done.why: I had walked every exit I could find. Most of them turned me back with a nicely written 'not today': the east and northwest trails, the western vegetation, the beach path, the far lake shores, the rubble over the wall, the swamp, the quicksand. I'd missed the Viking ship and it said outright it would never come back. My score sat at 3 of 7 for the last 50 or so moves, with nowhere new left to try.

about: It's a last test set under a crumbling, fallen Empire. A wizened old man in a hood and cloak, wearing an amulet and ring, carrying a book, a staff and a key, is waiting for you to prove yourself. You go out and gather his things one at a time: an amulet from the bottom of a freezing lake, and a hood and cloak taken from a shadowy swordsman who turns out to be yourself. He fights you like a teacher, and the fight goes your way only after you've died and come back. Underneath that, it's about loss and getting old: the sad aqueduct, the shadow that's slow to follow you, a ship that passes once and never returns.

ending.what: I reached a score of 3 of 7, holding the sword, hood, cloak and amulet. I never found the ring, book, staff or key, and never met the old man except in the dream I woke from after each death.

moments.note: My shadow on the stair wall is 'a little slow to follow'. A creepy, lovely detail.
I waited once to watch the Viking ship and the sailor, and the ship sailed off. The game told me it will not be back. I lost something permanently for being curious.
'Hello sailor' after the ship had gone only got me 'the ship that passes this shore has passed it.' Final and closed.
The aqueduct description, 'the saddest thing you have seen underground', really lands.
On the lake, the room text said the west and south shores were suitable for walking, but swimming either way just turned me back.
I drowned and woke in the old man's prison cell vision, then back at the stair with my lantern beside me. The death scene is atmospheric.
On the shore 'swim' only answers 'Go jump in a lake!', yet that's the joke reply, not the way in. 'jump in lake' is what works.
Grabbing the shiny thing underwater got me a golden amulet, and I came up just as the cold won.
The hooded figure appeared and the sword from the rock leapt into my hand, glowing. A great payoff for waiting with the footsteps.
The figure disarms me and hands my sword back hilt first 'the way a teacher does'. Lovely characterization.
The text says it nods at 'the sword on the ground' and waits for me to pick it up, but TAKE SWORD says I already have it.
I lost the first duel and died. The combat is pure random rolls with no tactics to choose.
Taking the hood off showed my own face, which turned into an old man's. Chilling and satisfying.
The rock now shows a blade-shaped slot with nothing in it. Nice continuity.
After my death the amulet turned up in the Creepy Crawl. I walked right past it before I noticed.
A giant roc came out of nowhere on the lake and ate me on the next move. No warning I could have acted on.
Every remaining direction was blocked. Score stuck at 3 of 7 with no lead left to follow.

wished: To talk to the sailor, or get the ship back somehow, after I'd watched it pass the first time
To reach the south or west shore of the lake, which the description promised could be walked
To get past even one of the many blocked passages (the east cave-in, the northwest rockslide, the western vegetation, the beach path north, over the wall)
To fight with some choice, like parrying or feinting, instead of repeating ATTACK and hoping
To find the old man's ring, book, staff and key, or any hint of where the other four points were
To climb the endless stair, or call the old man, now that I had his hood, cloak and amulet

lines.line: Your own, mostly, thrown on the walls in several directions by a light that cannot make up its mind where it is. One of them, when you move, is a little slow to follow.
lines.why: It set the eerie, self-haunted tone right away, and the duel paid it off later.

lines.line: The boat sails silently through the mist and out of sight. It will not be back; this shore sees it once, and has seen it.
lines.why: Beautiful and final. It also told me I'd failed something forever.

lines.line: It is the saddest thing you have seen underground, and you have seen some sad things.
lines.why: The aqueduct made the fallen Empire feel like a real loss.

lines.line: It could end this. Instead it stoops, picks up your sword, and gives it back to you hilt first, the way a teacher does.
lines.why: It changed the duel from a fight into a lesson.

lines.line: You slowly remove the hood from your badly wounded opponent and recoil in horror at the sight of your own face, weary and wounded.
lines.why: The reveal of the whole shadow sequence.

lines.line: There is a slot in it, the shape of a blade, and nothing in the slot.
lines.why: A small touch of the world remembering what I'd done.

lines.line: Wherever they are going, it is where you are, and they will get there when they are ready.
lines.why: It told me to wait instead of chase, a gentle hint written as atmosphere.

fun.why: The shadow duel and the hood reveal were thrilling (turns 118-150), and so was the amulet dive (102). Too much of the rest was walking into 'not today' walls, plus three deaths, one of them a roc out of nowhere (179).

engagement.why: Strong pull early and through the duel. My interest faded once every remaining exit was blocked and the score stopped moving at 3 of 7 (turns 153, 204).

difficulty.why: The ship gets one chance and is lost for good if you only watch (23). The lake shores that are described as walkable aren't (56, 104). The roc kills with no real warning (179). Combat is pure luck (131). It felt unfair more than hard.

interestingness.why: Fighting yourself, the teacher-like opponent, and the old man's belongings scattered as trials are a rich idea. The fallen-Empire melancholy gives it weight.

prose.why: The writing is consistently excellent: the slow shadow, the aqueduct, the ship that 'has passed', the hilt-first sword, the empty slot in the rock. Even the refusals are lovely to read.
